content: Catamenial pneumothorax is a medical condition characterized by the collapse of a lung that occurs in association with menstrual periods. The term catamenial specifically refers to menstruation. This condition is thought to be primarily caused by endometriosis involving the pleura, which is the membrane surrounding the lungs. Catamenial pneumothorax is the most common manifestation of thoracic endometriosis syndrome. Other forms of this syndrome include catamenial hemothorax, catamenial hemoptysis, catamenial hemopneumothorax, and endometriosis-related lung nodules. Rare and atypical presentations of thoracic endometriosis syndrome have also been documented. Endometriosis can attach to the lungs, forming cysts that resemble chocolate in appearance. While the parietal pleura is most commonly affected, other areas such as the lung tissue itself, the visceral pleura, the diaphragm, and, in rare cases, the tracheobronchial tree may also be involved. The exact mechanism by which endometrial tissue reaches the thoracic cavity remains unclear, although defects in the diaphragm are frequently observed. These cysts can release blood, essentially menstruating within the lung. Additionally, air can enter the pleural space through mechanisms that are not yet fully understood, contributing to conditions like catamenial hemopneumothorax. Epidemiological data suggest that catamenial pneumothorax accounts for approximately 3-6% of spontaneous pneumothorax cases in women. Given that spontaneous pneumothorax in women occurs at a rate of about 1 in 100,000 per year, this condition is exceedingly rare. As a result, it is often omitted from standard medical textbooks, and many physicians are unfamiliar with it. However, it is likely underdiagnosed and underrecognized in clinical practice. The onset of lung collapse in catamenial pneumothorax typically occurs within 72 hours after the start of menstruation. It is most commonly observed in women aged 30-40 years but has been reported in younger girls as early as 10 years old and in postmenopausal women. The condition is almost exclusively seen in women of reproductive age, with many patients having a history of pelvic endometriosis. Diagnosis may be suggested by a high recurrence rate of lung collapse in women of reproductive age who have a known history of endometriosis. Laboratory findings may include elevated levels of CA-125, a marker that can be associated with endometriosis. Pneumothorax is a medical emergency due to the associated severe pain and compromised lung function. Initial management involves the insertion of a chest tube following clinical assessment. This intervention allows the release of air and menstrual blood from the pleural space, enabling the lung to re-expand. Surgical removal of endometrial tissue is often recommended and should ideally be performed during menstruation to optimize visualization of the cysts. Pleurodesis, a procedure to adhere the lung to the chest wall, may also be beneficial. Hormonal therapies can be used to suppress menstruation and prevent recurrent lung collapse. Options include medications such as leuprolide acetate (Lupron Depot), danazol, or extended-cycle combined oral contraceptive pills. A combination of surgical and hormonal treatments has been proposed, with varying outcomes in terms of both shortand long-term effectiveness.
